We had a customer at @ListKitio  that wanted to only run outbound cold email campaigns a couple of times per year because their business is seasonal. They sell fundraising products to schools.

In June/July you're building demand and booking commitments for August

In September/October you're following up with August customers AND warming up December prospects

In January/February you're following up with December customers AND booking March

In April/May you're following up with March customers AND already locking in August for next year

There is no off-season.

There's just different parts of the demand gen flywheel.

Stack that on top of using our killer AI database search to expand their geographic reach and targeting entities other than schools that do fundraising and there's so much potential.

15,000 contacts into one vague campaign = one shot at mediocre resonance

The effort difference is minimal. You're already pulling the list. You're already writing copy.

"We'll make it up in volume."
lol

Email isn't the problem. Unwanted email is.

Nobody unsubscribes from "You just made a sale."
Nobody deletes "Your offer was accepted." 
Nobody ignores "The part you needed is back in stock."

Don't send unwanted email.

People don't hate email. They hate email that wastes their time.

Cold email gets lumped in with spam because most cold email acts like spam. Same templates. Same subject lines. Same "I help companies like yours" bullshit. Same ask for "15 minutes to chat."

But it doesn't have to be that way.

A cold email that intercepts the thought they already had, addresses the problem they're already dealing with, and offers something they actually want to see? 

That's not spam. That's relevance.

The recipient doesn't care that you've never met. They care whether you're wasting their time.

10 things you can pitch in a cold email OTHER THAN a call:

- Audit
- Free trial
- Loom video

- Sample deliverable

2. The identity story they tell themselves
3. The frustrations they're tired of explaining
4. Their quiet fears they don't admit publicly

6. What they already believe about solutions like mine

In conclusion, it's simple. Don't be selfish. Put in the work. Orchestrate intros. Do research before asking for help. Don't add overhead for people that you're looking for help from. Do that stuff and making and/or asking for introductions will be super-effective for you.

I'm often asked for this type of introduction: "hey, do you know any [people or companies] that [match this criteria]?" WTF? Why don't you do the work and then see if there's a legitimate reason I might know someone there - or know that person - and then ask me for an intro?

Okay, as for getting introductions, if you want someone to introduce you to someone they know, make a strong case for that. 

Why should they invest their social capital in you? That's what you're asking them to do, right? 

Relationships are super valuable. Respect that value.

And now that person you basically ambushed with your introduction looks bad and, by association, you also look bad. 

So avoid this by orchestrating the introduction appropriately. 

I'm not going to say this is common sense because it clearly isn't.

What kind of drama? Just because you're ready to make the intro doesn't mean the person you're emailing (while CC'ing the other person) is ready for the intro. Perhaps they have a full plate or are dealing with something outside of work/business and can't reply immediately.

Only after getting confirmation that both parties are open to an introduction should you make the intro. Regardless of your intentions, and regardless of how valuable this intro is for one or both, this type of surprise just adds overhead. Set it up first and avoid drama.

Before you introduce two people - in order to not look bad yourself (so consider this a selfish move if that motivates you) - contact both parties, find out if they're open to an intro (even - especially? - if this is a sales lead for them), and brief them on the other person.

So, let's talk about introductions - making them and asking for them - shall we? 

First, if you want to introduce someone to me, that's amazing; thank you for thinking of me. But I think there's a better way to do this that will make everyone involved look better. Here we go.
